synthesis.summary: Tom, you are right, and it is not one mistake but several that stack. (1) The pane is 72% white. That is more opaque than any glass I found in any source (the highest was 60%; ordinary glass panes run 10-30%), so it hides the room instead of showing it. (2) The room behind it is already blurred and almost a single blue, so there is nothing sharp for the glass to soften: the pane's 28px blur changes the photo by about 5 brightness levels out of 255, and after the 72% fill only about 1.5 of those survive. (3) The cards inside the pane carry their own glass setting, and it does nothing. A browser rule says anything inside an element that has backdrop-filter cannot see the page behind it, so the cards are just more white paper. I reproduced that in Chromium. (4) The pane covers 82% of the window and has a thick white frame, so it reads as an app window with a pale skin, not a slab of glass standing in a room. Glass reads as real when you can see something sharp and colourful cross its edge and turn soft, when the pane is mostly see-through (fill roughly 10-30%), and when the edge catches light from one side like a thin bevel. Apple's name for the part we are missing is lensing, light bending at the edge. Plain CSS cannot do lensing. Chrome can fake it with an SVG filter, and Safari cannot as of today (the WebKit fix is still unmerged on 2026-11-02). So the honest target is convincing frosted glass in every browser, with true edge refraction as a Chrome-only extra on the corner objects. The fonts are a separate cause: the page sets -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased (it comes from the Vibe component library), which makes Chrome on a Mac draw text about 12% lighter, and the text is mostly 12-14px. Both are fixable below, but nobody has yet rendered the fix on Tom's own 1080p screen, so treat the numbers as a tested starting point, not a finished design.

diagnosis.title: The pane is 72% white, so it hides the room instead of showing it
diagnosis.why: A fill of rgba(238,245,255,.72) lets only 28% of what is behind it through. Measured at the left edge of the pane on a 1920x1080 screen, the visible edge is made by the fill (brightness jumps 59-101 levels) and not by the blur (0-9 levels), so the eye reads a pale card laid on a photo. The highest fill I found in any source is 60% (Comeau's thicker-glass demo, kube.io's music player). Ordinary glass panes run 10-30%: Malewicz's generator 15%, Setproduct 12%, web.dev and NN/g 30%, KeyShot 10%, and liquid-glass-react uses no tint at all. The tint is also pre-blued (238,245,255), so the little that gets through is pushed toward the same pale blue. Apple does make glass more opaque for text-heavy parts, which is why text belongs on cards and not on bare glass.
diagnosis.fix: Pane fill = diagonal white gradient .34 to .14 to .26 (average about .24), neutral white, with blur(18px) saturate(1.6) brightness(1.04). Put all text on flat cards at .58-.62 white so legibility does not depend on the pane. Full numbers in recipe_css.

diagnosis.title: The room behind the glass has nothing in it to blur or bend
diagnosis.why: scene.webp is 1664x1024 (so it is also upscaled on a 1920 screen), already Gaussian-blurred, and squeezed into one hue band (201-220 degrees) and one narrow brightness range. Re-measured: blur(28px) removes about 5 of 255 brightness levels from it, and after the 72% fill only about 1.5 remain, which is invisible. Malewicz, whose article started the style, says the backdrop 'can't be too simple or dull, or the effect won't be visible' and needs clear tonal differences. Apple's guidance limits the clear, see-through variant to visually rich backgrounds. Fairness note: this is a partner to cause 1, not the only cause. Over the same photo a thin-fill pane already shows windows and light shapes, and Tom's own reel sits on a soft blue office, so fix both. In my renders, either fix alone looked more like glass than the shipped build, and both together looked clearly best.
diagnosis.fix: Stop pre-blurring and pre-grading. Use a sharp backdrop with at least three hue families, a dark area and a bright area, and 3-5 hard-edged shapes that cross the pane's edge with 40-60% of each shape under the pane. See the backdrop field for the build.

diagnosis.title: The cards' own glass is dead code, and the entrance animation fades the pane's glass
diagnosis.why: By the CSS Filter Effects spec, an element with backdrop-filter becomes a 'backdrop root', and any backdrop-filter inside it can only see what is painted inside it. Card.module.css puts blur(16px) on cards that sit inside the pane, which has its own blur. In headless Chromium 153 and 156 a child's blur under a backdrop-filter parent stayed pixel-sharp, and with the child's filter present the card ended up whiter, not more glassy. Counting the fills, only .28 x .28 = 7.8% of the room can reach a card. The variable --glass-card-blur is used, but it has no effect. The same rule bites in a second place: an ancestor with opacity below 1 removed all the blur in my test (opacity .97), and the pane's 900ms entrance runs opacity .5 to 1, so the glass is faint while it plays. A WebKit engineer confirmed the same rule for Safari. Apple also says never to put glass on glass.
diagnosis.fix: Delete backdrop-filter from .card. Give cards a flat fill (.58-.62 white). Put the pane's backdrop-filter on its own empty layer that is a sibling of the content, with no ancestor that has opacity below 1, filter, mask, clip-path, mix-blend-mode or will-change. Animate the entrance with transform only and end at transform: none.

diagnosis.title: The pane fills the window, so it reads as an app window, not a glass object in a room
diagnosis.why: At 1920x1080 the pane is 1792x952, which is 82% of the screen; the room shows in 17.7% of the area. In the audit's measurement the cards cover about 85% of the pane, so the glass itself shows only in the margin strip and the gaps. Apple's guidance is that glass is a floating layer for controls and navigation above content, not the content layer, and Microsoft says not to put acrylic on large background surfaces. Both are about this exact pattern. That is what Tom means by 'it just sits in the browser'.
diagnosis.fix: Inset 88px at 1920x1080 (pane becomes 76% of the screen, with room visible all round), corner radius 44px (Tom's second reference is about 48px), 24px gutters between cards so the glass shows between them, and concentric card radius = pane radius minus padding (20px). Keep it ONE pane: Setproduct says two stacked glass panels usually look worse, and Microsoft warns that side-by-side panes leave a visible seam. The rail gets a flat fill, not its own glass.

diagnosis.title: The edge is a thick white frame with no thickness cues, and true lensing is missing
diagnosis.why: Apple says lensing is the primary way Liquid Glass defines itself, and that bigger glass is simulated as thicker material with deeper shadows and stronger bending. Ours stacks a 1.5px .88-white border, a 4px gradient ring that never fades out on the unlit sides (it is already directional, so 'uniform' was wrong, but it is 4px thick), a 6px band, a 7px blue line and a 40px inner glow that sits over real content. That reads as a picture frame. The outer drop shadow (0 40px 90px, .45) is present and heavy, so shadow is not the problem. The implementations that look right use a 1-1.5px lit edge that fades to nothing on the dark side: liquid-glass-react uses a 1.5px ring, KeyShot a 1px border plus a small offset inset highlight. Comeau adds a 4-6px edge strip with its own blur and brightness to fake thickness. Lensing itself needs an SVG feDisplacementMap used as backdrop-filter: url(), which only Chromium draws. WebKit bug 245510 is still open and its three fix pull requests were unmerged on 2026-11-02, so Safari and Firefox get no lensing.
diagnosis.fix: Replace the ring stack with: 1px border at .35, one 1.5px masked ring that is bright top-left and fades to zero (the recipe has it), KeyShot-style small inset highlights, one soft inner shade at the bottom, and a layered shadow tinted to the backdrop. Delete the 40px inner glow. Add real lensing only on the corner objects, Chrome and Edge only, with a plain-blur fallback.

diagnosis.title: The three corner objects read as app-icon tiles, not glass
diagnosis.why: They are filled 40-66% white, their blur(12px) works on an already-blurred room so it does nothing, and at 89-131px they are small. Refraction is the cue that tells the eye an object is glass, and it is cheapest and most visible on small objects. Figma's own Glass effect lists refraction at the edges, depth and dispersion as its controls, which is the same ingredient list as Apple's.
diagnosis.fix: Fill .10-.30 white, 160-220px (19vmin), radius 28%, each one straddling the pane's corner so half is sharp in the room and half is blurred under the pane, with a sharp coloured shape behind it. Then, in Chrome and Edge only, give them the SVG lens filter described in recipe_css.

diagnosis.title: Fonts: macOS is told to draw the thinnest text, and the type is small and regular weight
diagnosis.why: The body sets -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased through Vibe's own token. In Chromium on a Mac that value switches off font smoothing and hinting, and Skia's comments say smoothed text is drawn from outlines that CoreGraphics thickens while unsmoothed text is not. On Tom's Mac (macOS 26.6.2, a Philips 221V8LB at about 102 ppi, which macOS treats as 1x) I re-ran a probe: smoothing on draws 13-23% more ink, with no colour fringing. Measured with Figtree in Chrome, antialiased 400 has 0.88 of the ink of default 400, antialiased 500 is about default 400, and default 500 is 1.13x. The CSS has 35 declarations at 14px and 32 at 12px, only 5 at 16px and 1 at 28px, and Figtree's x-height is just 0.500 em (7px at 14px, 6px at 12px). Apple says to avoid light weights and to go larger with thin type. Honest limit: this was measured in headless Chrome on synthetic specimens, nobody has compared the real dashboard with the flag removed, and the glass layer itself did not thin text in my tests.
diagnosis.fix: Remove antialiased, and override the Vibe token on :root, because Vibe applies it in 62 places. Body 15px/500, titles 18px/600, KPI numbers 40px/700, nothing below 13px except uppercase labels. Ink #0f172a and #1e293b. Details in type_scale.

synthesis.backdrop:
What must be behind the glass: something sharp, colourful and varied, because glass is only visible by what it does to something. Targets, measured against today's photo. Hue spread: at least 100 degrees across three families (today one band, 201-220 degrees). Brightness: from a dark area around 25% lightness (a navy shape) to a bright area around 95% (today a narrow pale band, roughly 40-95% of range). Detail: hard edges and shapes between 4 and 40px across, so an 18px blur has something to soften. Shapes: three to five, 220-420px at 1080p, with 40-60% of each shape under the pane and the rest sharp outside it, so the eye sees sharp turn to soft across the same edge. Source resolution at least 2560px wide if it is a photo (today 1664). Do not blur, bloom or grade it in advance; the pane does the softening.

Option A, built in code (my recommendation for the light, pastel look of Tom's second reference and for the reel's bright feel). It costs no download, stays sharp at any resolution, and is the version I rendered and saw working (the audit's strongest result). On .env use: linear-gradient(120deg, #6b7dff 0%, #b48cff 45%, #ff9ec4 75%, #7cd4ff 100%) as the base, plus four radial-gradient blobs on top (pink #ffb3d9 near the top left, sky #8fd3ff near the top right, violet #b9a2ff near the bottom right, mint #7ee8d0 near the bottom left, each about 55-60% wide fading to transparent at 60%). Then add hard-edged shapes as absolutely positioned divs sized in vmin so they scale: a white ring about 30vmin across at the top left corner, a navy (#1b2a6b) rounded square about 26vmin on the right edge, a yellow (#ffd45e) capsule about 34vmin by 13vmin rotated -18 degrees at the lower left, a coral (#ff6e64) circle about 24vmin at the bottom right corner, and a green (#3ddc97) bar about 40vmin by 7vmin tilted 8 degrees along the top edge. Put a small inner highlight on each (a radial-gradient white at 35%) so the blurred part under the pane still reads as volume. Place the three .gobj glass objects on top of the shapes at the pane's corners. With the pane inset at 88px, the pane edges sit at x=88 and x=1832, y=88 and y=992, so shapes must cross those lines.

Option B, a photo (for the dark, warm look of Tom's first reference: lamp light, window, bokeh). It must be sharp: a real photo of a living room with warm lamp points and a cool window, or one generated in FLUX.2 klein through Draw Things at 2560x1440 with the steps raised to 10-12 so the edges are crisp. Do not run it through blur, bloom or a single-colour grade. Export WebP at about quality 85 and keep it under about 400KB. With a dark photo, switch the pane to a dark fill: background rgba(12,14,20,.34), backdrop-filter blur(20px) saturate(1.6), border 1px rgba(255,255,255,.16), white text; bright points under the pane bloom into soft discs, which is what sells it. Warning from LogRocket: dark glass over a too-dark photo is invisible, so the photo needs bright points.

How to check it worked (my own heuristics, not from a source): turn the pane's fill to zero and compare brightness just outside and just inside its edge; the average difference should be at least 8 levels (today 0-13). And (1 minus fill) times the detail the blur removes should come to about 5 levels or more (today 0.28 x 5 = 1.5).
synthesis.type_scale:
Smoothing (do this first, it is the single biggest text change): delete -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased. Set  :root{ --font-smoothing-webkit:auto; --font-smoothing-moz:auto; }  and  body{ -webkit-font-smoothing:auto; -moz-osx-font-smoothing:auto; }  because Vibe applies its token in 62 places, so removing it from body alone is not enough. Do not use text-rendering: geometricPrecision; Blink turns hinting off for it too. Quick proof before committing: in Chrome DevTools add that :root override and compare the page at 1920x1080 with it on and off. If antialiased must stay for some reason, add 100 to every weight and 1px to every size, because antialiased 500 only matches default 400. Note that Josh Comeau's widely copied reset keeps antialiased on purpose; that is a Retina-era choice and this monitor is not Retina.

Sizes and weights for Figtree on a 1920x1080 non-Retina screen (about 102 ppi):
- Page title: 28-32px, weight 700, line-height 1.15, letter-spacing -0.02em. (Tom's first reference uses a 56px headline on a hero; a dashboard needs less.)
- KPI numbers: 40px, weight 700, line-height 1.1, letter-spacing -0.02em, proportional figures. Use tabular-nums only inside tables, because Figtree's tabular '1' leaves a wide gap (a '1111' measures 66px proportional but 100px tabular at 40px).
- Card titles: 18px, weight 600, line-height 24px (second reference: 18-20px semibold).
- Body and table rows: 15px, weight 500, line-height 22px, colour #0f172a.
- Secondary text: 13px, weight 500, line-height 18px, colour #1e293b, no added letter-spacing (Apple's table tightens slightly at 13pt, it does not open). Floor of 13px for anything meant to be read.
- Uppercase labels only: 12px, weight 600, letter-spacing +0.06em, colour #1e293b.
- Never 12px/400 slate text, which is what a lot of the page is today.

Colours: fully opaque ink only, no rgba text. #0f172a for primary, #1e293b for secondary. I replaced #334155 because over a thin pane the audit measured it dropping to 3.7-4.8:1 in the worst spots. Contrast I computed for the recipe (pane about .24 white plus card .60 over the darkest backdrop spot, a navy shape): #0f172a about 9.3:1, #1e293b about 7.7:1. Accent colours do not survive small: over that same dark spot #1d4ed8 gives about 3.5:1 and #15803d about 2.6:1, so use accents only as chip fills, dots or numerals of 24px and up, with dark text beside them. Never put text straight on the bare pane; text lives on .card or .rail.

Font loading: Google Fonts serves one variable Figtree file for 400/500/600/700, so those cost nothing extra. To use in-between weights such as 450 or 550, change the request to family=Figtree:wght@300..900. Optional: Inter 500 for body-size text (x-height .546 against Figtree's .500, so it reads larger at 14-15px) and keep Figtree for titles and numbers.

Keep the text sharp: no will-change: transform on any element that holds text (Drawer.module.css line 26, KatieStage.module.css and MotionStage.module.css all set it, so check the open drawer), end every entrance animation at transform: none, use whole-pixel insets (88px, not percentages), no opacity below 1 on text containers at rest. Check the result on the real 1080p monitor, not a Retina laptop.
synthesis.risks:
1. Nothing here has been rendered on Tom's own screen. My renders were in headless Chromium 153/156 with software compositing, the GPU path was never tested, and nobody has compared the real dashboard with the font flag removed. Apply the structure fix, take a 1920x1080 screenshot in Tom's Chrome, and tune the fill (.14-.34) and card (.58-.62) numbers by eye.
2. Expect frosted glass, not Apple's Liquid Glass. Real lensing is Chromium-only, WebKit bug 245510 is open and its fix pull requests (68614, 68613, 69566) were still unmerged on 2026-11-02, so any Safari, iPad or iPhone viewer sees the CSS-only version. Make sure that version looks good on its own, because practice owners and reps will not all use Chrome. I could not verify what browser Tom uses; a 1080p monitor says nothing about it.
3. A WebKit bug (297620, status NEW) stops backdrop-filter from working at all when it uses var() on macOS 14 Safari. The recipe uses literal numbers for that reason. Tom's Mac (macOS 26) is not affected, but other viewers could be.
4. Text on a thinner pane has less contrast. The recipe protects it by putting all text on cards at .58-.62 white, and I computed 7.7:1 or better for #1e293b over the darkest spot, but I only computed it for a few sample backdrop colours, not the final art. Re-measure against the real backdrop. Apple's own guidance is to avoid content crossing glass in steady states, and NN/g recommends simple backdrops for legibility; the shapes-crossing-the-edge look comes from the references, not from a rule.
5. I could not open either Dribbble shot or the Instagram reel. Every figure about them (about a third opaque, 40% white pane, 50-60% cards, 48px radius, 40px numbers, 56px headline) comes from Tom's description, unverified. A skeptic who looked at the reel's saved frames in the repo (docs/research/glassy-reference/ and docs/screenshots/glass-v2/reel-vs-ours-1440.png) read it as a thick, tilted slab with a lit side wall, refractive cubes and a floor reflection on a soft blue office, with near-opaque pale cards. That is a visual read, not a confirmed fact, and the reel's tooling is unknown. If Tom wants that exact look, thickness (side wall, tilt, reflection) may matter more than anything in the recipe, and that is a separate piece of work from this one.
6. SVG refraction maps must match the element size exactly and be rebuilt when it changes; they cost most when the backdrop changes (ours is static); and sharp map edges can look jagged (a low-confidence claim, the source page would not open). Use it on three small objects only. Do not animate blur radius.
7. Keep blurred elements few: one big pane plus three small objects is fine. Do not add glass back to cards. If cards ever need to show the room, that requires a second sibling glass layer, and Apple advises against glass on glass.
8. The 'dark glass' variant (Tom's first reference) can vanish over a dark photo (LogRocket); it needs bright points in the photo.
9. The entrance animation changes from a 900ms opacity-plus-tilt to a 500ms transform-only tilt. If Tom wants a fade, fade .pane-content (cards and text), never .stage or .env.

'Larger glass should have a perspective tilt, side wall, refractive cubes and floor reflection, as in the reel' is a skeptic's visual read of saved frames. The reel's tooling is unknown, and I could not open the reel.

Tier 3 (baking the refraction into a pane-sized image offline) is a proposal with no source describing it. The claim that SVG displacement maps do not super-sample and look jagged is source-unreachable (the Medium page returned 403).

audit.summary:
Tom is right, and the cause is not the blur setting. The glass has nothing to refract and is too opaque to show it. Real glass reads as glass when four things hold. (1) Something sharp, high-contrast and multi-hue sits behind the pane, and you see it crisp outside the pane and soft inside it, across the same edge. (2) The fill is thin, about 10-45% white, so that thing dominates the pane's colour (web.dev's frosted pane is 30%, NN/g's example is 30% with 25px blur). (3) saturate/brightness lifts the colour so the blur does not go muddy. (4) The edge is lit from one direction, bright on the top-left and shaded on the bottom-right, with a sheen and a soft shadow. Apple describes the real thing as bending and concentrating light, not just scattering it (WWDC25 session 219, https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2025/219/). We fail (1) and (2) badly, (3) and (4) partly, and a bug makes the cards worse than a plain fill.

Ranked by how much each explains the verdict:
- Backdrop with nothing in it: the room is pre-blurred, one blue hue, and squeezed into a narrow tonal range.
- Slab and card fills at .72, with the card fill sitting on the slab fill.
- Card backdrop-filter inside the slab's backdrop root, which blurs nothing and whitens the cards.
- A 64px frame of room around a pane that covers 82% of the window.
- A directionless edge.
- Corner objects that read as app-icon tiles.
- Type: `-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased` plus light, small, 12-14px text with no display tier. This one explains the fonts half of the verdict only.

I rendered the old recipe and a fixed recipe side by side in headless Chromium 153 on this Mac, in the scratchpad only. No SAIDA files were touched.
- Scratchpad folder: scratch/glass-audit/
- V0_currentCss_sceneWebp.png is the current CSS replica, V1_currentCss_sharpRoom.png is the current CSS over a sharp vivid room, V2_fix_sharpRoom.png is the fix over that room, and V3_fix_sceneWebp.png is the fix over the existing scene.webp.
- The V1 vs V0 comparison isolates the room. The V3 vs V0 comparison isolates the glass recipe.
- Both V1 and V3 look more like glass than shipped. V2, where both change, is clearly the strongest.
- The V0 replica omits the rim and the corner objects, so it is close to the shipped build but not identical.
- I could not open either Dribbble shot: curl returned 0 bytes and WebFetch returned empty. Every reference number for them comes from Tom's description in the task, not from me.

One thing the audit must not hide: the fix makes text sit on a thinner, busier surface. Worst-case contrast in my prototype was 6.79:1 (vivid room) and 5.27:1 (scene.webp) for #1e293b, but only 4.8 and 3.73 for the current secondary ink #334155. The fix therefore has to darken secondary ink.

The 900 ms entrance (glass.css:342-359) uses opacity .5 and a transform only while it runs, and ends at `none`. `.env` and `.slab` are siblings, so the slab really does sample the room. A crisp light edge does exist: pixel profile at y=500 on overview-1920-demo.png is margin (99,143,181), then a 1px antialias step, then a 2px line at (239,246,253), then slab (205,225,248). verified.summary:
Citations hold up: I re-opened every source and almost all of them say what the researcher says they say. The two reachable-by-me exceptions are the original Malewicz URL (uxdesign.cc and Medium both return HTTP 403 for me too, so "identical text" on hype4.academy cannot be checked) and the Discourse thread (the researcher did not open it; I did, and it confirms the claim). I also re-measured scene.webp with ffmpeg and a small script, and my numbers match theirs within rounding. Hue is 201-220 degrees at p5-p95 with median saturation 0.38. A 28px Gaussian removes a mean 5.3 luma levels, which falls to about 1.5 after the 0.28 pass-through of the 0.72 fill. The luma jump at the slab edge is 62-102 levels with the fill and about 0-13 without it. The slab covers about 82 percent of a 1920x1080 viewport.

The problems are in the synthesis, not the quotes.
1. "Every source says" three things together is overstated. NN/g tells you to choose a simple or single-colour backdrop when you control it. Apple and Microsoft give no fill band at all. The 0.10-0.45 band is the researcher's own synthesis of tutorial recipes.
2. The researcher left out the canonical generator's strongest edge cue, an inset 20px glow with 10px spread at alpha 1.0. That undercuts "every recipe uses only a faint highlight, so our rim is over-built".
3. Comeau's production code uses a 0.5 header fill, not the 0.1 from his demo. His own fix for busy content is 0.6, and he never says that point stops being glass.
4. Three parts of the recipe contradict sources the researcher cites. A glass rail contradicts Microsoft's rule that vertical panes get opaque fills. "Keep the room visible" at blur 16-20px cuts against NN/g's more-blur-is-better stance. Using Malewicz's Dribbble warning against a desktop slab ignores that he scopes it to phone apps and says a desktop web interface could use glass for its backgrounds.
5. The details about Tom's reference images (amber lamp against blue window, 48px radius, 40px numerals, 50-60 percent white cards) carry no citation, and I cannot verify them.
6. The code path is src/shell/Shell.tsx, not src/components/Shell.tsx.

One possible cause the research never examined: WebKit bug 297620 (still open) breaks any var() inside backdrop-filter on macOS 14 Safari, and glass.css puts var() in every slab, card and object blur. It does not affect Tom's own Mac (Darwin 25.6, macOS 26), so I flag it as a candidate for other viewers, not as the cause.

I did not use any browser tools or edit any files under ~/Desktop/SAIDA. I only read glass.css, Card.module.css, Shell.tsx, Shell.module.css and scene.webp. Scratch files are in the scratchpad.

kept.claim: Malewicz names four traits: background-blur transparency, multi-layered floating objects, vivid colours, subtle light border
kept.note: Exact list is in the page. A plain fetch shows only the intro, because the body sits in an embedded JSON blob in the HTML, which I parsed. The uxdesign.cc and Medium originals return 403 for me too, so 'identical to the original' is unverified.

kept.claim: Malewicz: backgrounds can't be too simple or dull, can't be over-detailed, need tonal difference; Big Sur wallpaper is the example
kept.note: Quote: 'They can't be too simple or dull, or the effect won't be visible.' Also: 'make sure it has enough tonal difference.'

kept.claim: Malewicz: most prominent with at least two translucency levels on a busy colourful background; only the fill should be transparent, not the whole object
kept.note: Exact. The same passage also says the style 'can only use one transparent layer, or multiple', so one pane is legitimate. He also says closer objects are 'a bit more transparent', which matches the researcher's note.

kept.claim: Malewicz: 1px semi-transparent inner border simulates the glass edge (with/without comparison); his Dribbble critique says mockups cheat because full-screen apps have no visible backdrop
kept.note: Both are in the text (he typos '1p'). But the Dribbble critique is scoped to phone apps ('apps on phones are all full-screen'). He also writes that 'you could imagine a desktop web interface using a similar level of transparency for just its backgrounds' and that the style shines when used on just one element. The researcher's 'reality check' applied to a desktop dashboard slab overreaches.

kept.claim: Malewicz accessibility rules and 2021 update: not for buttons/toggles, fine for card backgrounds, contents must work without glass; real products moved to lower transparency, larger blur, higher text contrast; dark-mode variant has better contrast
kept.note: All present. 'Lower transparency' means more opaque, which pushes against a very low fill, and the researcher never says so. Tying this to 'Tom's dark-glass reference' is the researcher's inference.

kept.claim: Malewicz generator defaults: white 0.15, blur 20px, 1px border 0.3, shadow 0 8px 32px 0.1, inset top 0.5 and bottom 0.1, 1px top and left gradient lines peaking at 0.8
kept.note: Every listed value is correct. The researcher omitted a line in the same box-shadow: inset 0 0 20px 10px rgba(255,255,255,1), a fully white inner glow. The top line fades transparent to 0.8 to transparent horizontally; the left line runs 0.8 to transparent to 0.3 vertically. 'Top-left light source' is an inference, and the page does not say it.

kept.claim: NN/g definition: opacity plus blur; white 30% with 25px blur keeps edges somewhat distinguishable, 100px blends everything; strokes and gradients add depth especially on simple or one-colour backgrounds
kept.note: Matches the article. NN/g also says glass stands out in front of gradients or complex backgrounds, consistent with the researcher.

kept.claim: NN/g best practices: more blur than designers expect; Dribbble/Behance shots try too hard to keep backgrounds distinguishable; simple or single-colour backdrop acceptable if you control it; meet contrast, let users reduce transparency, use sparingly
kept.note: Source says 'More background blur is better' and criticises designs that 'try too hard to keep background elements distinguishable'; 'than designers expect' is the researcher's gloss. On backdrops the source is stronger than 'acceptable': 'if you have control of what appears behind a translucent component, opt for simple or single-color backgrounds.' That cuts against the recipe's 'keep the room visible' direction.

kept.claim: NN/g Liquid Glass critique: 'Transparency = Hard to See', text over text is illegible
kept.note: Section title and the line 'anything placed on top of something else becomes harder to see' are present, along with the caption 'Text on top of text creates an illegible mess.'

kept.claim: Axess Lab: bright backgrounds listed as a requirement; WCAG 4.5:1 and 3:1; never rely on blur alone; honour prefers-reduced-transparency; avoid blur(20px) and above
kept.note: All present. Bright backgrounds are listed as 'works best', not as a requirement. The article also lists Minimalism as an element. The 'avoid 20px+' advice is as the researcher says, and it conflicts with Malewicz's own 20px default.

kept.claim: Setproduct (June 2026): depth comes from what you partially see through; recipe fill 0.12, blur 16, border 0.25, radius 16; easy to produce, premium only on a controlled gradient, contrast fails on the next screen
kept.note: Published June 9, 2026. Recipe values and the quotes are exact.

kept.claim: Apple WWDC25 219: lensing is the primary way glass defines itself; edge highlights, colour spill, shadows; larger glass simulates thicker material; Apple did not try to recreate a physical frosted material
kept.note: Transcript says 'The primary way Liquid Glass visually defines itself is through ... Lensing', describes the highlights layer, light spilling from colourful content, and thicker, deeper-shadowed material at larger sizes. It also says 'rather than trying to simply recreate a material from the physical world'. The word 'frosted' is not used.

kept.claim: Apple HIG Materials: Liquid Glass is a functional layer for controls and navigation above content; not in the content layer; sparingly; regular variant for text-heavy components; clear only over visually rich backgrounds; 35% dimming layer; thicker materials more opaque
kept.note: Every point is in Apple's JSON for the page. Apple says the regular variant 'blurs and adjusts the luminosity' of background content, which a static fill cannot do (see missed list).

kept.claim: Microsoft acrylic: background, blur, exclusion blend, tint, noise; do not layer multiple acrylic surfaces; not on large background surfaces; opaque for vertical panes; no accent-coloured text
kept.note: Recipe and don'ts are correct. Two limits the researcher dropped: 'avoid layering' refers to multiple layers of background acrylic, and side-by-side panes are warned against because they leave a visible seam. The 'opaque for vertical panes' rule contradicts the researcher's own recipe, which makes the rail a glass pane.

kept.claim: Filter Effects Level 2: backdrop-filter, filter, opacity<1, mask, clip-path, non-normal mix-blend-mode make a Backdrop Root; backdrop-filter elements must form one themselves; effect invisible unless semi-transparent; opacity applies to the filtered backdrop
kept.note: All present, including that the Backdrop Root Image is content painted between the nearest ancestor Backdrop Root and the element. The spec also states it 'does not yet have Working Group consensus, specifically on the definition of Backdrop Root', which the researcher omitted. The effect on a card inside the slab is inferred, not tested in a browser.

kept.claim: MDN: backdrop-root list; a parent with opacity<1 makes a child's backdrop-filter blur only content between parent and child; frosted example white 30% blur(10px)
kept.note: The pitfall sentence is quoted nearly word for word. The example is rgb(255 255 255 / 30%) with blur(10px); MDN does not label it 'frosted'.

kept.claim: Discourse thread corroborates that a backdrop-filtered ancestor blinds backdrop-filtered descendants (Chrome, Edge, Safari), fix via ::before or siblings
kept.note: The researcher had not opened it; I did. A Discourse staffer states that an element with backdrop-filter 'becomes the root for the effect' and descendants 'can only blur what's inside that root', and gives the working fix: a ::before with the filter plus isolation:isolate. The thread tested iOS Safari and desktop Chrome; Edge is not mentioned. The thread is dated Sept 2026.

kept.claim: Comeau: only pixels directly behind are used; extend the filtered layer; 3-6px edge slice with blur 8px and brightness(120%); base fill white 0.1 blur 16px; fix busy text with blur 12px or fill 0.6
kept.note: All appear in the demos. But Comeau's own final production code uses a 0.5 header fill plus a 95%-lightness fading gradient, and its edge strip is blur(12px) brightness(0.96) at 4px. He presents 0.6 as a legitimate glass fix, so the researcher's 'point where it stops being glass' is the researcher's editorial, not his. Page updated Oct 2026; Chrome 142 fixed overflow:hidden for the extended-backdrop trick.

kept.claim: LogRocket: plain backgrounds hide the effect; Figma recipe white 0.45, border 0.25, blur 15; embossed inset option; the article contradicts itself on layer order
kept.note: All present. The self-contradiction is exact: the Hierarchy section says the nearest object is more opaque with higher blur; the Stacking section says the nearest has less opacity and less blur.

kept.claim: UX Misfit: shadow, differentiated blur, active layer more opaque, dim lower content, about 20% white stroke; deliberately gives no exact values
kept.note: All four steps and the 20% stroke are there, and so is the no-values disclaimer. It also says to avoid glass 'as the large parts of the UI', which supports the researcher's slab criticism and was not cited.

kept.claim: IxDF: muted pastel palettes work best, neutral text and icons; contradicts Malewicz and Axess on vivid backgrounds
kept.note: Pastel and neutral-text claims are present, as is the iOS 7 darkened-backdrop example. The 'contradiction' is overstated: the same page says the three key traits are 'transparency, light borders, and vivid or pastel colors' and requires tonal differentiation.

kept.claim: WCAG 1.4.3: 4.5:1 normal, 3:1 large; 18pt/14pt bold is about 24px/18.5px; test the worst-case backdrop region
kept.note: Thresholds and the px conversion are exact. The 'UI components 3:1' rule is SC 1.4.11, not this page. The worst-case advice is not in NN/g or Axess as attributed: NN/g only notes contrast may hold 'over certain areas'. The explicit worst-case phrasing is in the buildmvpfast article.

kept.claim: New Target (2025): thin fonts dissolve on frosted backdrops, bolder hold; 20-30% dark overlay under text; '85-90 percent' figure unclear
kept.note: Matches, including the ambiguous '85-90%' wording ('modest level of opacity reduction (such as 85-90%)'). Dated Aug 21, 2025.

kept.claim: Eidos Design and Setproduct agree on a 'cheapness' failure: beauty over clarity, and the effect breaks once real content replaces a controlled mockup gradient
kept.note: Eidos supports 'beauty over clarity' and 'a returning trend isn't innovation', and nothing about cheapness or mockup gradients. The 'controlled gradient' point is Setproduct's alone.

kept.claim: MEASURED: scene.webp is 1664x1024, 18,078 bytes, hue 201-220 (p5-p95), median saturation 0.38; Gaussian 6 removes 1.2 luma levels, blur 28 removes 4.9 (p99 24.6), only 1.4 (p99 6.9) after the 0.72 fill

kept.note: Reproduced at heights 200/400/540/700/900: outside 103/140/158/138/112, inside 205/215/220/214/211, jump 62-102, blur-only change 1-13. kept.claim: CODE FACT: Card.module.css gives .card backdrop-filter blur(16px) saturate(1.1) and a 0.72 fill; cards render inside the backdrop-filtered .slab, so the slab is their Backdrop Root and only 0.28 x 0.28 = 7.8% of the room reaches a card
kept.note: Code facts are correct, and the arithmetic is right. 1. Nested backdrop-filter. Over striped stripes, a child with blur(10px) inside a parent that also has backdrop-filter shows no blur at all. The same child under a plain parent blurs correctly. This confirms the researcher's "cards inside the slab do nothing" claim (nested.png).
2. The remedy, which the researcher did not give: put the slab's backdrop-filter on a ::before/sibling layer instead of the slab itself, and the child's blur works again (nested2.png). A parent opacity of .99 does not change anything.

The archisvaze SVG refraction at IOR 1.5 also works in this Chromium and adds visible edge bending and a rim, though subtly on such a soft photo (refract.png). verified.summary: The core mechanism holds up. Blink maps -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased to grayscale AA with hinting off, and CoreGraphics only dilates (fake-bolds) text in the non-antialiased path. I re-ran the Swift probe on this Mac (macOS 26.6.2, no AppleFontSmoothing set globally or for Chrome): smoothing ON draws 13-23% more ink, with no colour fringes. I also recomputed the Figtree ink ratios from the saved Chrome bitmap fs/out6.bmp: antialiased 400 is 0.87-0.88 of default 400, antialiased 500 is about 1.00, default 500 is 1.13, and each +50 of weight adds 6-6.6%. Independent sources agree (Chromium/Skia source and comments, Ben Wagner, a Mozilla engineer's bug comment), so that part is solid. Several things the owner should NOT take as fact. (1) "Main cause" is asserted, not shown: nobody A/B-tested the real dashboard with antialiased removed; the evidence is synthetic specimens and ink ratios. (2) "The dashboard's own CSS has no will-change" is false: Drawer.module.css:26 (the 560px text drawer), KatieStage.module.css:29 and MotionStage.module.css:79 all set it; the researcher only grepped glass.css and global.css. (3) The "glass layer doesn't thin text" tests ran in software-composited headless Chromium only; the GPU-on and GPU-off bitmaps are byte-identical, so no GPU path was tested. (4) "Mostly 14px/400 and 12px/400" is overstated: the dashboard CSS has 22 font-weight 500, 15 at 600 and 3 at 700 declarations, and about 30-37% of the 14px and 12px rule blocks already set 500/600; the "BEFORE" specimen is a hypothetical all-400 card, not what ships. (5) 12% less ink is about two 50-unit steps, not one, and by the researcher's own table antialiased 400 reads like default weight ~305-310, not ~350. (6) The Skia "loses the contrast boost" inference is wrong: contrast is 0.0 on Mac in every path, so only the gamma pre-blend is skipped. (7) Google Fonts serves one variable woff2 for all four weights, not separate files. (8) The contrast numbers assumed a #f8fafe card; on the actual shipped photo under the 72% white card, ink #0f172a and slate #334155 still pass comfortably (median 14.3:1 and 8.3:1), but accent blue #2563eb is about 4.1:1 and green #16a34a about 2.6:1. (9) The recipe's "+0.005em tracking at 13px" and "72% white (Apple)" have no Apple support: the HIG macOS tracking table is -0.006em at 13 pt, and Apple gives no opacity figure.

kept.claim: Blink on macOS maps -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased to no smoothing and turns hinting off.
kept.note: CreateSkFont: kAntialiased sets should_smooth_fonts=false (edging kAntiAlias, grayscale); hinting set to kNone for antialiased or geometricPrecision (crbug 152304). 'Lightest possible' is interpretation; kNoSmoothing is aliased, not lighter by ink.

kept.claim: Skia CoreText backend: hinting-none avoids CG outline dilation; smoothed text is drawn from auto-dilated outlines, regular AA from un-dilated ones.
kept.note: Comments near lines 910-929 say exactly this, and line 984 says 'CoreGraphics dialates smoothed text to provide contrast'. Comments are old but my probe reproduces the effect on macOS 26.6.2.

kept.claim: Chromium Mac builds SK_GAMMA_CONTRAST=0.0 without SK_GAMMA_APPLY_TO_A8, so antialiased text also loses the contrast boost; Windows uses 1.0.
kept.note: Facts check out (BUILD.gn is_mac: SK_GAMMA_SRGB + CONTRAST=0.0; is_win CONTRAST=1.0; ignorePreBlend() for unhinted A8; APPLY_TO_A8 only defined for Android), but the conclusion fails: contrast is 0.0 on Mac in both paths (the smoothed path also calls setContrast(0)), so there is no contrast boost to lose. Only the luminance/gamma pre-blend is skipped, and no source says whether that thins or thickens. The Skia code even carries a 'Do we want contrast boost?' TODO.

kept.claim: Ben Wagner: CoreGraphics dilates smoothed outlines by a percentage set by AppleFontSmoothing; antialiased is how web developers avoid it; dilation 'should have been reduced as the font size increased'.
kept.note: All three points are in the 2012 message. It also says Chromium builds A8 from LCD so transparent or animated text stays dilated, and that AppleFontSmoothing 0 takes the regular path.

kept.claim: Skia was patched in 2018 because Mojave text came out too thin, and now probes CoreGraphics for none/some/subpixel; modern macOS gives 'some', so Chrome on Mac never draws LCD text.

The 'modern macOS gives some / never LCD' step is not in this source; it rests on the local probe, which I re-ran (no colour fringe in any row).

kept.claim: Local CoreGraphics probe on Tom's Mac: smoothing ON draws 13-23% more ink than OFF, no colour fringes; Avenir Next Regular 14px gains 22.6%, about two thirds of the jump to Medium.

kept.claim: Chrome headless, real Figtree, 1x: antialiased 400 has 0.88 of default 400's ink; +50 weight is about 6.5-7%; antialiased 500 is about default 400; default 500 is 1.13x; so 400+antialiased reads like a weight around 350.

kept.note: Doc says accent text is 'likely to not pass' contrast at 14px (softer than 'fail'); the hyperlink advice has no stated reason.

kept.claim: NN/g and Axess Lab agree on WCAG contrast (4.5:1 body, 3:1 large/UI), sampling real colors behind glass, semi-opaque fills; they disagree on blur.
kept.note: NN/g: 'More Blur Is Better' and the WillowTree sampling plugin; Axess: 4.5/3, semi-opaque fills, avoid blur(20px) and higher. Real disagreement. Note the dashboard slab and drawer use blur(28px).

kept.claim: Contrast is not the problem: #0f172a about 17:1, #334155 about 9.9:1, #64748b 4.55:1, green 3.15:1, amber 2.06:1 against about #f8fafe.
kept.note: Ratios recompute exactly, but #f8fafe was assumed. I sampled the shipped scene.webp under the real 72% white card: bg luminance median 0.79; #0f172a median 14.3 (worst 11.9), #334155 median 8.3 (worst 6.9), accent #2563eb median 4.1 (below 4.5 on much of it), #16a34a median 2.6. #64748b is not a dashboard token, and glass.css already uses #15803d for green text. The dashboard's own docs/perf/contrast.json (2026-10-27) reports pass=true. Conclusion holds for ink/secondary text only.

kept.claim: Chromium disables LCD text for will-change: transform, transform animations, filters, non-integral translation, non-opaque background; a backdrop-filter with more than one operation disables LCD text for layers behind it.
kept.note: ComputeLCDTextDisallowedReason lists all of these; FilterOperations::AllowsLCDText returns false for >1 op (and for saturate >1); draw_property_utils.cc UpdateRenderTarget propagates it to earlier effect nodes. Moot on Mac.

kept.claim: In Chrome tests, backdrop-filter, plain transforms, opacity .99, translateZ(0) and perspective rotateX did not change text sharpness; only will-change with fractional translate and rotation blurred it (dark pixels 1022 to 681, edge/ink 0.914 to 0.635); the glass layer is not what thins the text.
kept.note: Recomputed from out2/out3 bitmaps: only the will-change + .5px + rotate row degrades (edge/ink 0.973 to 0.694, -29%); antialiased plain 1016 dark px vs backdrop row 993. Big limit: out3_gpu_on.bmp and out3_gpu_off.bmp are byte-identical (cmp), so no GPU compositing path was tested; the conclusion holds only for software-composited headless Chromium.

kept.claim: will-change: transform rasterizes once into a fixed bitmap; use only for 60fps animation and remove afterward.
kept.note: Chrome blog says exactly this.

kept.claim: The dashboard's own CSS has no will-change, and the tilt entrance ends at transform:none.
kept.note: Tilt end state is right (glass.css keyframes 'to { transform: none }', fill backwards). But will-change: transform is declared in Drawer.module.css:26 (the 560px text drawer, with backdrop-filter), KatieStage.module.css:29 and MotionStage.module.css:79; only glass.css and global.css were grepped. The drawer's open transform is translateX(0), integer, so blur is unlikely, but it was not tested.

kept.claim: Apple fits glyphs to the pixel grid less than Windows, so it stays truer to the typeface but looks fuzzier; on a 1x monitor this shows soft thin stems.
kept.note: The 2007 essay says Apple preserves the typeface 'even at the cost of a little bit of blurriness'. But Joel argues Apple's rendering keeps text darker and truer to print than Microsoft's thinner snapped stems, which cuts against 'thin stems'; it also predates Mojave, so 'mechanism still applies' is the researcher's inference.

kept.claim: Tom's display is a Philips 221V8LB: 21.5 inch, 1920x1080, about 102.46 ppi, VA, 250 cd/m2; macOS sees 1x.
kept.note: Star Tech spec table lists 21.5", 1920x1080, VA, 102.46 PPI, 250 cd/m2. system_profiler here shows PHL 221V8LB, 'UI Looks like 1920 x 1080 @ 100 Hz'. 'Half the density Apple assumes' is arithmetic inference (about 102 vs about 218 ppi).

kept.claim: Before/after Figtree card: BEFORE 14/400 antialiased, 12/400, KPI 28/600; AFTER 15/500 default, 13/500, KPI 40/700; AFTER body has about 47% more ink per line.
kept.note: Image exists and matches. 47% is arithmetic (1.13 x (15/14)^2 / 0.88 = 1.47), not a pixel count. BEFORE is a hypothetical all-400 card, not what ships (many rows already use 500/600).

missed: Independent corroboration on post-Mojave macOS: Mozilla engineer Jonathan Kew (bug 1802795, comment 10) says removing -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased 'makes the text look significantly heavier'. https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1802795

Zach Leatherman: grayscale anti-aliasing 'makes things appear lighter and thinner', and the safe approach is to leave smoothing at platform defaults and override only as a last resort. Easy secondary support for the fix. https://www.zachleat.com/web/font-smooth/

Counter-position the owner should know: Josh Comeau's widely copied CSS reset ships -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased on purpose (Retina-era reasoning) and says Chrome and Safari 'still use subpixel antialiasing' on macOS by default. That wording conflicts with the researcher's probe (no colour fringe on macOS 26.6.2), but the practical effect is the dilation. The recipe is a trade-off aimed at a 1x monitor, not a universal fix. https://www.joshwcomeau.com/css/custom-css-reset/

No A/B on the real dashboard was shown: nobody rendered katie-dashboard with antialiased removed and compared it with the current build, so 'main cause' is an inference from synthetic specimens. The dashboard also already measures real-pixel contrast (pass=true): docs/perf/contrast.json

Three will-change: transform declarations exist in the dashboard (the text Drawer, KatieStage, MotionStage) and the Drawer was never tested for text blur at its open and mid-transition states. src/components/Drawer.module.css

The dashboard's real font request returns one variable Figtree file for all four weights, so intermediate weights (450/550) need wght@300..900 in index.html, and the researcher's 'separate files' statement is wrong. https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Figtree:wght@400;500;600;700&display=swap

Apple's own Liquid Glass drew heavy legibility criticism (text over busy backgrounds, low contrast), which supports raising card opacity and weight rather than treating thin text as a Chrome quirk. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/liquid-glass/
